question: How common is it, right now, and in whom?

vandenbroucke2007.cite: Vandenbroucke et al. (2007). Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE): explanation and elaboration. PLoS Medicine 4: e297.
vandenbroucke2007.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC2020496) on 20 Nov 2026; the article is online-only, so places are given as its STROBE items and boxes; in-text reference numbers are left out. The card's own reference (Wang & Cheng 2020, Chest) is not open access and was not read

steps.title: Draw a sample
steps.text: Define the population you want to describe and draw a sample from it by a plan written in advance: simple random, or in stages and strata.

quotes.text: Most cross-sectional studies use a pre-specified sampling strategy to select participants from a source population.

steps.title: Measure once
steps.text: Measure everyone in the sample at the same time, exposure and outcome together. There is no follow-up.

quotes.text: In cross-sectional studies, investigators assess all individuals in a sample at the same point in time, often to examine the prevalence of exposures, risk factors or disease.

steps.title: Count who answered
steps.text: Count how many were invited, eligible and measured. If those who answer differ from those who don't, the estimate drifts away from the population.

quotes.text: Those included in a study often differ in relevant ways from the target population to which results are applied. This may result in estimates of prevalence or incidence that do not reflect the experience of the target population.

steps.title: Estimate prevalence
steps.text: Divide the number who have the condition by the number measured. Correct the precision for the sampling design, not just the sample size.

quotes.text: They may examine the number of people who have a disease at a particular time (prevalence), or that develop a disease over a defined period (incidence).

steps.title: Compare groups
steps.text: An analytical survey compares prevalence between exposed and unexposed people. It shows an association, but not which came first.

quotes.text: Such studies may be analysed like a cohort study by comparing disease prevalence between exposure groups.

reverse-causation.text: A difficulty that can occur in any design but is particularly clear in cross-sectional studies is to establish that an exposure preceded the disease
